questions.prompt: What does it mean for two pieces of text to have similar embeddings?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: That the embedding model learned to represent them as semantically related, placing them near each other in the vector space

Embedding similarity reflects learned semantic relatedness according to the training process — it says nothing directly about factual truth, authorship, or exact wording.
keyPoints: Embedding similarity reflects learned semantic relatedness according to the training process — it says nothing directly about factual truth, authorship, or exact wording.

questions.prompt: Why might a general-purpose embedding model underperform on a specialized domain like legal or medical text?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A model trained mostly on general web text may not capture the specific vocabulary and semantic relationships that matter in a specialized domain, echoing the domain-mismatch concern from the Hugging Face course

Just as a general-purpose language model can underperform on specialized text, an embedding model's training data determines what kinds of semantic relationships it captures well — a mismatch with a specialized domain's vocabulary and concepts can hurt retrieval quality.
keyPoints: Just as a general-purpose language model can underperform on specialized text, an embedding model's training data determines what kinds of semantic relationships it captures well — a mismatch with a specialized domain's vocabulary and concepts can hurt retrieval quality.

questions.prompt: Why can't a single cosine similarity number (like 0.75) be assumed to mean 'a good match' across every embedding model and task?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The practical meaning of a given similarity score depends on how that specific model's embedding space is shaped and what the task actually requires, so it varies across models and tasks

Since different embedding models produce differently-shaped similarity distributions, the same raw score can represent a strong match in one context and a weak one in another — there's no universal cutoff that applies everywhere.
keyPoints: Since different embedding models produce differently-shaped similarity distributions, the same raw score can represent a strong match in one context and a weak one in another — there's no universal cutoff that applies everywhere.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental tradeoff that approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search makes?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: ANN search accepts occasionally missing the absolute best match or slightly reordering results, in exchange for search times that scale far better than linear brute-force comparison

The core tradeoff is speed for exactness: ANN methods give up a guarantee of finding the perfect top matches every time, in exchange for search performance that scales far better than brute force at large data volumes.
keyPoints: The core tradeoff is speed for exactness: ANN methods give up a guarantee of finding the perfect top matches every time, in exchange for search performance that scales far better than brute force at large data volumes.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a bare ANN index algorithm and a production vector database?
questions.referenceAnswer: The ANN algorithm (like HNSW or IVF) is the core search technique, while a full vector database adds everything needed to run that technique reliably in a real system: persistence, querying, concurrency, and operational tooling.
keyPoints: The ANN algorithm (like HNSW or IVF) is the core search technique, while a full vector database adds everything needed to run that technique reliably in a real system: persistence, querying, concurrency, and operational tooling.

questions.prompt: Why do very large vector collections eventually need to be sharded across multiple machines?
questions.referenceAnswer: Sharding exists specifically to address the point where one machine's resources are no longer enough — splitting the collection so each machine holds and searches only a manageable portion of the total data.
keyPoints: Sharding exists specifically to address the point where one machine's resources are no longer enough — splitting the collection so each machine holds and searches only a manageable portion of the total data.

choices.text: Sharding is always required regardless of collection size

At a large enough scale, a single machine's memory and compute aren't sufficient to hold the index and serve queries with acceptable latency, so the collection needs to be split across multiple machines
Sharding has no relationship to memory or compute constraints
A single machine can always handle any size vector collection with no limit

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind hybrid search?
questions.referenceAnswer: Hybrid search deliberately runs both search paradigms and combines them, aiming to get BM25's precision on exact matches together with embeddings' ability to find semantically related content that doesn't share literal wording.
keyPoints: Hybrid search deliberately runs both search paradigms and combines them, aiming to get BM25's precision on exact matches together with embeddings' ability to find semantically related content that doesn't share literal wording.

choices.text: Using only BM25 and ignoring embedding-based search entirely

Running both lexical (BM25) and embedding-based semantic search on the same query and combining their results, to catch both exact-term matches and semantically related content that lacks exact wording overlap
Using only embedding-based search and ignoring lexical search entirely
Hybrid search refers to combining two different embedding models, not lexical and semantic search

questions.prompt: Why does switching to a new embedding model require re-embedding the entire existing collection?
questions.referenceAnswer: As established early in this course, each embedding model defines its own distinct vector space — mixing old and new model embeddings in the same comparison is meaningless, making a full re-embedding of existing data a genuine requirement, not an optional step.
keyPoints: As established early in this course, each embedding model defines its own distinct vector space — mixing old and new model embeddings in the same comparison is meaningless, making a full re-embedding of existing data a genuine requirement, not an optional step.

choices.text: New embedding models are always compatible with embeddings from any other model, no re-embedding needed
Different embedding models produce incompatible vector spaces, so previously stored embeddings from the old model are meaningless when compared against new embeddings from the new model
Re-embedding is only needed if the new model has more dimensions than the old one
Vector spaces from different models are always directly comparable without any conversion
